title: Equation (10): the two models, and a confound worth noticing

what.formal: Equation (10) defines the paper's two models in two lines: $\mathrm{HGNN}\big(\varphi_r(X, T),\, H\big)$ for RD-HGNN, and $\mathrm{HGNN}\big(\psi(\varphi_r(X,T),\, \varphi_s(X)),\, H\big)$ for DD-HGNN. Both receive the incidence matrix $H$ and run the same network layer, Equation (1); they differ only in what arrives as the feature matrix.
what.plain: RD feeds the network the rule embedding alone. DD feeds it the fused vector — rule embedding plus structure. Same network, different input.

what.tex: \begin{aligned} \mathrm{HGNN}\big(\varphi_r(X, T),\; H\big) &\qquad \text{// RD-HGNN} \\[6pt] \mathrm{HGNN}\big(\psi(\varphi_r(X, T),\; \varphi_s(X)),\; H\big) &\qquad \text{// DD-HGNN} \end{aligned}
what.note: Read the two lines against each other and the difference is exactly one term: $\psi$, the fusion, which is what brings $\varphi_s$ — the structural embedding — into the picture.

gloss.md: the rule embedding $X_r$, from the boosted ensemble $T$ and the features $X$
the structural embedding $X_s$ — written here as a function of $X$ because the paper passes the whole dataset; what it actually reads is $H$
the incidence matrix, supplied to the network in both models
the network: Equation (1) applied as many times as there are layers

what.md: **The naming, decoded.** *Rule-Driven* means the model's input is the rules and nothing else. *Dual-Driven* means both kinds of knowledge drive it. And because the fusion is Equation (9), DD's input is $\tilde{X}_r \Vert X_r$, while RD's is just $X_r$.

**Here is a confound the two-line form makes visible, and it matters for reading the ablation.** RD's network input has $C_r$ columns; DD's has $2C_r$. So switching from RD to DD changes two things at once — it adds the structural knowledge *and* it doubles the width of the first weight matrix. If DD beats RD, part of the gain may come from the extra capacity rather than from the structural information. A clean ablation would compare DD against a model with the same $2C_r$ input and no structural content — for instance $X_r \Vert X_r$, whose degeneracy the previous card established — or against a version where the broadcast scalar is a learned per-vertex parameter rather than a degree-derived one. **The paper runs neither comparison.** This does not invalidate its result; it bounds what the result can be said to show.

**One more thing worth being precise about: RD is not structure-free.** Both models pass $H$ to the network, so in RD the structure still enters — through the smoothing, exactly as in every prior hypergraph network. What RD omits is the structure *as an explicit feature*. The word "Rule-Driven" therefore means "rules are the only embedded knowledge", not "the model ignores the graph". A reader who takes it the second way will misread the whole ablation.

example.md: **Walk 1 — trace what each model's network actually sees.** Use the two-tree ensemble from Figure 2, so $C_r = 5$, and a vertex with rule row $X_r[v] = (0,\; 0.5,\; 0,\; 0.5,\; 0)$ and structural value $X_s[v] = 0.9526$.

items.md: Compute DD's input. $\tilde{X}_r[v] = 0.9526 \times (0,\; 0.5,\; 0,\; 0.5,\; 0) = (0,\; 0.476,\; 0,\; 0.476,\; 0)$, and concatenating with the original gives ten entries.
items.why: The scaling acts on the whole row at once — the per-row-scalar property from Equation (9). Entries that were zero stay zero, so for a sparse rule row the scaled copy is *also* sparse, and half of DD's input is zero.

items.md: Note the width difference: 5 columns against 10.
items.why: With $d$ output channels, RD's first layer has $5d$ weights and DD's has $10d$. The extra $5d$ parameters exist whether or not the structural knowledge in them is useful — which is precisely the confound.

items.md: Now ask the ablation's question in the form that would settle it: would $X_r \Vert X_r$ — same width, no structural content — match DD?
items.why: It would not, by the argument of the previous card: concatenating a row with itself collapses to a single linear reading. So the width alone cannot explain DD's advantage *in full* — but the comparison needed to establish that is a model with the same width and a non-redundant, non-structural second block, which the paper does not run.

example.md: **What Chapter 6 will therefore be able to say, and what it will not.** The DD-versus-RD gap is evidence that the combination helps, given the architecture. It is not clean evidence that *structural knowledge* is what helps, because width and content moved together. Whether that gap is larger on datasets with bigger hyperedges — which is the paper's own prediction — is a separate and more informative check, and it is the one to look for in the results tables.

quiz.q: Which term distinguishes the two models in Equation (10)?

opts.expl: Both lines call the same function on the same incidence matrix. If the networks differed, the comparison would not isolate the knowledge encoders.

opts.md: The fusion $\psi$, which is the only thing bringing the structural embedding into DD's input
opts.expl: Correct. Remove $\psi$ and both lines become identical — RD is literally DD with the fusion and the structural encoder deleted. That is what makes RD a clean test of the rule encoder alone.
Both models are given $H$. RD is not structure-free: it still smooths along hyperedges, exactly as the prior literature does. What it lacks is structure *as a feature*.

quiz.q: If $C_r = 12$ and the output width is $d$, how many weights does DD's first layer contain, in terms of $d$? Give the answer for $d = 1$.
quiz.hint: The input width is twice the rule width; a layer with $d$ outputs has input-width times $d$ weights.
quiz.sol: $2C_r \times d = 24 \times 1 = 24$ weights for $d = 1$. RD's corresponding layer would have $12$. The doubling is a direct consequence of the concatenation in Equation (9) and is the reason the confound exists: DD is not just RD plus information, it is RD plus information *and* capacity.

quiz.q: DD's input in the walkthrough is half zeros. What does that imply for the confound?

opts.md: The confound disappears, since zero entries carry no capacity
opts.expl: The entries carry no *information*, but the weight matrix still has a column per input entry — those parameters exist and are trained, whether or not the corresponding inputs are usually zero.

opts.md: The confound is softened but not removed: the extra parameters are trained on inputs that are often zero, so they may end up doing little — but the paper reports no experiment separating the two effects
opts.expl: Correct, and this is the honest position. A sparse input means some of the extra capacity is idle, which weakens the alternative explanation without eliminating it. The only way to settle it is the comparison the paper omits — same width, no structural content — which is exactly the kind of gap Chapter 7 collects.

opts.md: It means the fusion is wasted work
opts.expl: Not wasted: the nonzero rule entries are genuinely reweighted by the structural value, which is the mechanism the design intends. The observation is about how much of the *width* is informative, not about whether the scaling does anything.

close: **Next:** the paper's own discussion of which model to choose — Section IV-D-2, where it states a prediction about when each variant should win, and which dataset property it expects to drive the difference.
